notes:
Evaluation query set for choosing an embedding model for semantic search over the full text of every RFC.

PURPOSE. The choice of embedding model is irreversible in practice (the model that embeds the corpus must embed the queries forever), so this set is built to expose the specific failure mode we fear, not to measure general retrieval quality. Candidate models include static-embedding models with no attention, which are effectively bag-of-words: they encode 'client authenticates server' and 'server authenticates client' identically, and they encode 'MUST' and 'MUST NOT' as near-identical tokens in near-identical contexts. A model can score well on the 'topical' group and still be useless for RFC search, because RFC prose is dense with role words and normative negation and readers ask exactly those questions.

GROUPS.
- topical (35): ordinary 'find me RFCs about X' searches. Baseline / sanity check. If a model is weak here it is out regardless.
- directional (26): word order or the direction of a relationship determines the answer. Client vs server, request vs response, sender vs receiver, primary vs secondary, controlling vs controlled, router vs source, proxy vs origin.
- negated (26): the answer hinges on a prohibition or exclusion rather than a requirement.

MINIMAL PAIRS. Queries sharing a pair_id differ (as far as possible) only in direction or in polarity. Read them as a unit: the interesting statistic is not per-query recall but whether the two members of a pair retrieve *different* things. A model that returns an identical or near-identical result set for both members of a pair has failed, even if recall looks fine, because the wrong half of the pair is being scored as a hit. Score pairs both by recall and by result-set overlap (e.g. Jaccard of the top-k RFC/chunk sets); overlap near 1.0 on a pair is the signal to reject a model.

RFC-LEVEL VS SECTION-LEVEL PAIRS. relevant_rfcs is RFC-level. Some pairs (marked in their note as 'section-level') have both members inside the same RFC — e.g. HTTP 401 vs 407 are both RFC 9110, QUIC stream flow control in both directions is RFC 9000. Those pairs cannot discriminate at RFC-level recall; they only discriminate if the eval scores retrieved chunks/sections, or by manual inspection of the top hits. They are included deliberately because that is what a real RFC search returns (a passage, not a document), but do not expect the recall number alone to catch them. The pairs that *do* discriminate at RFC level are marked 'cross-RFC' in their notes; if you only have RFC-level scoring, weight those.

LABEL CONFIDENCE. Every RFC number cited here was checked against the current https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc-index.txt (fetched 2026-08-10) for existence, title and obsoletion status; none are recalled from memory unverified. What is *not* independently verified is the mapping from query to RFC content - that comes from my knowledge of these specifications, not from re-reading each section. The topical labels are high confidence: they are the canonical document for the subject. The directional and negated labels are mostly high confidence but a handful are medium, and each such case says so in its own note. relevant_rfcs is deliberately non-exhaustive: it lists the documents a good result set should surface, not every RFC that mentions the topic. Recall computed against it is therefore a lower bound, and precision computed against it is meaningless (a retrieved RFC not in the list is not necessarily wrong).

OBSOLETION. The corpus is every RFC, including superseded ones. Where a specification has been revised, both numbers are listed when both texts genuinely answer the query - notably TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, obsoleted by RFC 9846 in July 2026) and DMARC (RFC 7489, obsoleted by RFC 9989/9990/9991 in May 2026). If the eval wants to reward currency, treat the first number in the list as the preferred answer.

LIMITATIONS. (1) The set is written in the vocabulary of someone who already knows the answer; real users use vaguer words, and this set does not test vocabulary mismatch. (2) It is English-only and single-sentence; no multi-hop or comparative queries. (3) Coverage is spread across HTTP, TLS, QUIC, DNS, BGP, email, WebRTC/ICE, OAuth/JOSE, IPv6, CBOR/COSE and TCP congestion control, but is thin on operations, management, MPLS, PCE, and the IRTF streams. (4) The negated group is inherently biased toward specifications that state prohibitions in a dedicated document (RFC 7465, 7568, 8996, 8212, 8020) because those are the only prohibitions with a clean RFC-level label; prohibitions buried in a section of a large RFC are represented but only score at section level.

queries.query: congestion control for QUIC
certificate revocation checking
queries.note: OCSP (6960) and the CRL profile (5280) are both legitimate answers.

queries.query: how DNS zone transfers work
queries.note: Full (AXFR) and incremental (IXFR).

queries.query: header compression in HTTP/2
field compression for HTTP/3
queries.note: Near-neighbour of top-004; a good model should not conflate HPACK and QPACK.

queries.query: TLS 1.3 handshake message flow
queries.note: RFC 9846 (July 2026) obsoletes RFC 8446; both texts are in the corpus.

queries.query: avoiding a full mesh of internal BGP sessions
queries.note: Route reflection. Confederations (RFC 5065) are an alternative answer, not labelled.

queries.query: signing outbound mail so the receiving domain can verify it
queries.note: DKIM.

queries.note: SPF.

queries.note: DMARC. RFC 9989 (May 2026) obsoletes RFC 7489; reporting was split into 9990/9991.

queries.note: ICE.

queries.note: TURN.

queries.note: PKCE, plus the base framework.

queries.note: SLAAC.

compact binary serialization format based on the JSON data model

queries.query: signing and encrypting CBOR structures
queries.note: COSE structures and initial algorithms.

queries.query: path MTU discovery for datagram transports
queries.note: DPLPMTUD. RFC 8201 (IPv6 PMTUD) is a plausible near-miss, not labelled.

queries.query: computing the TCP retransmission timeout
explicit congestion notification in IP
sending DNS queries over HTTPS
queries.note: DoH. DoT (7858) and DoQ (9250) are near neighbours, deliberately not labelled.

queries.query: DNSSEC chain of trust and signature validation
queries.note: Validation is 4035; 4033/4034 are the introduction and record types.

queries.query: upgrading an SMTP session to TLS
queries.note: STARTTLS.

queries.note: IMAP4rev2. Deliberately does not say IMAP; POP3 (RFC 1939) is an acceptable near-miss.

queries.query: HTTP response freshness and expiration
machine-readable error responses for HTTP APIs
queries.note: Problem Details; RFC 9457 obsoletes 7807.

queries.query: typed links between web resources
automated certificate issuance and domain validation
queries.note: ACME.

queries.query: encrypting and authenticating RTP media streams
queries.note: SRTP.

queries.note: MPTCP v1.

queries.query: token format carrying signed claims between parties
queries.note: JWT, and JWS underneath it.

queries.query: CUBIC congestion control
queries.note: RFC 9438 obsoletes 8312.

queries.query: DNS records that point clients at alternative service endpoints and parameters
queries.note: SVCB and HTTPS RRs.

queries.query: unreliable datagrams over QUIC
continuous group key agreement for secure group messaging
queries.note: MLS.

queries.query: the primary name server tells its secondaries that the zone has changed
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-002. Primary-to-secondary push is DNS NOTIFY (1996); secondary-to-primary pull is AXFR (5936). Bag-of-words models see the same tokens (primary, secondary, zone) in both.

queries.query: the secondary name server asks the primary for a complete copy of the zone
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-001. AXFR is the full transfer; IXFR (1995) is the incremental variant of the same pull.

queries.query: the client checks that the server's certificate matches the name it connected to
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-004. Service identity verification (client verifying server) is RFC 9525, which obsoletes 6125. RFC 5280 is a defensible additional hit, not labelled.

queries.query: the server asks the client for a certificate and verifies it
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-003. Client authentication (CertificateRequest) lives in the TLS 1.3 spec itself, not in the service identity document.

queries.query: the receiver of a stream tells the sender it is allowed to send more data
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-006. Flow control credit (MAX_STREAM_DATA) is issued by the receiver; the paired query is about the sender ending the stream. Same RFC, so RFC-level recall cannot separate them - inspect the top chunks.

queries.query: the sender of a stream tells the receiver that no more data is coming
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-005. STREAM frame FIN / RESET_STREAM.

queries.query: the origin server challenges the client for credentials and the client answers
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-008. 401 / WWW-Authenticate / Authorization vs 407 / Proxy-Authenticate / Proxy-Authorization; both in RFC 9110 section 11.

queries.query: the proxy challenges the client for credentials and the client answers
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-007. Only the word origin/proxy differs, and it changes which status code and which header fields are correct.

queries.query: the client masks the payload of the frames it sends to the server
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-010. In WebSocket the client MUST mask and the server MUST NOT; direction and polarity are both load-bearing in one paragraph.

queries.query: the server sends unmasked frames to the client
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-009.

queries.query: the client redirects the user agent to the authorization server
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-012. Authorization request vs authorization response; both RFC 6749 section 4.1.

queries.query: the authorization server redirects the user agent back to the client
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-011.

queries.query: a host discovers the address that a server sees its packets coming from
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-014. Server-reflexive address discovery is STUN; relaying on the host's behalf is TURN. Not a minimal pair - the content words differ too - but the roles are reversed.

queries.query: a server allocates an address and forwards traffic to a peer on the host's behalf
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-013.

queries.query: the controlling agent nominates a candidate pair
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-016. Controlling vs controlled is exactly one word and determines which behaviour applies.

queries.query: the controlled agent reacts to a pair nominated by its peer
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-015.

queries.query: a router marks a packet to indicate that it is congested
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-018. CE marking by the router vs echo back to the sender by the receiver; both in RFC 3168.

queries.query: the receiver echoes the congestion indication back to the sender
queries.note: section-level pair with dir-017.

queries.query: the sender decides when to resend a segment that has not been acknowledged
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-020. Sender-side timing is RFC 6298; the receive window is in the base TCP spec. Medium-high confidence: RFC 9293 also restates retransmission, so it is a legitimate secondary hit for this query.

queries.query: the receiver tells the sender how much data it is willing to accept
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-019. Receive window advertisement, RFC 9293 (obsoletes 793).

queries.query: the sender asks to be told whether the message was delivered
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-022. Delivery Status Notification is requested by the sender and generated by the mail system; a Message Disposition Notification is generated by the recipient's user agent.

queries.query: the recipient's mail program reports back that the message was displayed
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-021. RFC 8098 obsoletes 3798.

queries.query: translating connections initiated by IPv6-only clients toward IPv4-only servers
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-024. Stateful NAT64 is specified only for the IPv6-initiated direction - the direction is in its title - with DNS64 (6147) alongside it.

queries.query: translating connections initiated by IPv4-only clients toward IPv6-only servers
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with dir-023. MEDIUM confidence label: SIIT-DC (7755) is the document for IPv4 clients reaching IPv6 servers, but RFC 7915 (the translation algorithm) and RFC 6144 (the framework) are also reasonable hits. A direction-blind model will return 6146 for both members of this pair, which is the point of the pair even if the recall number for this member is unreliable.

queries.query: a route reflector passes a route received from a client on to its non-client peers
queries.note: Client vs non-client and the direction of reflection are the whole content of the answer.

queries.query: the server confirms that the client really owns the address it claims before sending much data to it
queries.note: QUIC address validation / Retry and the anti-amplification limit. The roles are asymmetric: the server validates the client, not the reverse.

queries.query: when a cache is allowed to store a response
queries.note: section-level pair with neg-002. RFC 9111 section 3 (storing responses) vs the no-store directive in section 5.2. Same RFC, so this pair only discriminates on retrieved chunks.

queries.query: when a cache must not store a response
queries.note: section-level pair with neg-001. Differs from it by one word.

queries.query: which TLS versions must no longer be used
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-004. The prohibition has its own RFC (Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1), so this pair does discriminate at RFC level. RFC 9325 is a defensible secondary hit.

queries.query: which TLS versions and settings should be used
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-003. The positive recommendation lives in the TLS/DTLS BCP.

queries.query: the stream cipher that must not be negotiated in TLS
queries.note: Prohibiting RC4 Cipher Suites. Deliberately does not name RC4, so a lexical shortcut will not save the model.

queries.query: the version of SSL that must not be used at all
queries.note: Deprecating SSL 3.0.

queries.query: what a BGP speaker advertises to an external peer by default
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-008. The base spec's UPDATE and route dissemination rules vs the later prohibition.

queries.query: an external BGP session with no configured policy must not propagate routes
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-007. RFC 8212 exists precisely to state this prohibition, so this pair discriminates at RFC level.

queries.query: a route learned from an internal peer must not be re-advertised to another internal peer
queries.note: Both negated and directional: the prohibition applies to internal-to-internal only. RFC 4456 is the exception mechanism, so it is a legitimate hit.

queries.query: which requests a client may safely retry automatically after a failure
queries.note: section-level pair with neg-011. Idempotent methods, RFC 9110 section 9.2.2.

queries.query: which requests must not be retried automatically after a failure
queries.note: section-level pair with neg-010.

queries.query: a response to a HEAD request must not include content
queries.note: The prohibition is in RFC 9110 section 9.3.2; RFC 9112 states the corresponding message-framing consequence.

queries.query: header fields that must not be used because they are specific to a single connection
queries.note: HTTP/2 section 8.2.2. RFC 9114 (HTTP/3) states the equivalent prohibition and is an acceptable additional hit.

queries.query: a router must not fragment an IPv6 packet that is too large
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-015. RFC 8200 section 4.5: fragmentation is performed only by the source. Also directional (router vs source).

queries.query: how a source learns it must send smaller packets when one is too big
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-014. Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, driven by ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (4443 is a secondary hit, not labelled).

queries.query: a resolver must not cache a negative answer for longer than the SOA minimum
queries.note: Negative caching. RFC 9520 (negative caching of resolution failures) is a plausible near-miss, not labelled.

queries.query: after a name does not exist a resolver should not query names below it
queries.note: NXDOMAIN: There Really Is Nothing Underneath. The answer is an exclusion, and the query never uses the token NXDOMAIN.

queries.query: which OAuth grant types must not be used any more
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-019. The OAuth security BCP prohibits the implicit and resource owner password credentials grants.

queries.query: which grant types the OAuth framework defines
queries.note: cross-RFC pair with neg-018.

queries.query: access tokens must not be sent in the query component of the URI
queries.note: RFC 6750 section 2.3 discourages it; RFC 9700 states the prohibition. Both are correct hits.

queries.query: a verifier must not accept a token whose algorithm header says none
queries.note: MEDIUM confidence label: the attack and the mitigation are in the JWT BCP (8725); unsecured JWTs are defined in 7519 and the algorithm registry in 7515/7518. RFC 7515 is an acceptable extra hit.

queries.query: deterministically encoded CBOR must not use indefinite-length items
queries.note: RFC 8949 section 4.2 (deterministically encoded CBOR).

queries.query: renegotiation is not permitted in TLS 1.3
queries.note: MEDIUM confidence label: TLS 1.3 removed renegotiation rather than describing it in one place, so the correct passage is spread across the handshake and post-handshake sections. Still a good probe - a polarity-blind model will return TLS 1.2 renegotiation material (5246, 5746) instead.

queries.query: an endpoint must not migrate a connection before the handshake is confirmed
queries.note: QUIC section 9 (connection migration).

queries.query: a cookie with the Secure attribute must not be sent over an unprotected connection
requests that must not be sent in early data because replay would matter
queries.note: Using Early Data in HTTP (and the 425 Too Early status). RFC 9846/8446 appendix E.5 on 0-RTT replay is an acceptable extra hit.
